speaker: Speaker 1
words: Someone was telling me that your father worked in the woods or during the big fire in 1910.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, he served as a cooker in a fire in the creek. He would cook sometimes. He cooked at the Ole Miss in 1910, around 1900. Ole Miss is down here. Around 1900, he was the main... And he got to be cooked for the Polaski's crew. The Polaski's crew.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And he was out in the woods during this awful bad fire season.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, he was. He was a cooker who went up on the mountain. And he went way up on the mountain from the fire. He was a cook. And his crew was a miner. And the fire went over. Would you give him any tips?

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So he was in... I've read some in a book about some of those miners were killed. Some of the men were...

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, that's more...

speaker: Speaker 1
words: That must have been a terrible experience. Do you remember the fire?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, I remember. We were over the fire with my mother. And we homesteaded on the Truett Creek. And my mother had to go down the mountain and get the horses and bring them in. And she buried the dishes in the garden. More than a man could do. She got a sewing machine in the back of a wagon. And she went down the Truett Creek that way with Lenore and I. I remember. He was a... I had a stroke at one point. Two dribbles. Can't tell you too much.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But it was... Was the house burned?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: No, it didn't get down anymore.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Uh-huh. They just expected it to.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Yes, they had thick cinders falling in the yard. And they got out. There was no man available to help. Mother had to do it all by herself.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And she had two little girls. But she managed to hitch up the horses and got away. They got out?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Uh-huh. And she stayed down at the... And she didn't hear from Dad for a long time. And the fire was over. And they told Daddy to get home. He had given the man $5 for the money to go down and tell Mother that she was all right. And he would go back up and do some more work for some of y'all. And this man told you he was the first to go in and he was born in New York.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: And he never did get the message to your mother. So it was a long time that she didn't even know that he was gone. That must have been a really terrible experience.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, it was a terrible experience. Everybody had multiple times. Uh-huh.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: But your father survived.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes. Dad was all right. He was all right. And when they... And this fellow up there, he was pretty good when they came out. So many of them were such mother fakes that he volunteered to go down to Kingston to walk and tell the people. They wouldn't believe he was involved in magic. The cinders and everything. When he ran down that mountain, the fire would stir up in the cinders behind him. And he went down the... The fire went down that way. Uh-huh. And they wouldn't believe him. But the mayor of the town of Walnut said that anything Dad said was all right. So Dad... Then they sent a crew up to help. They put Dad to bed. And he slept the clock around.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Just exhausted.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: And we... And then, it must have been after that that they went back up there with a lot of horses. And they supplied some help to the men that were up on the mountain.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: They took doctors and medical aid up there. When you were growing up in your family, did you do things together as a family?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Oh, yes.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: What kind of activities did you enjoy?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, we... Dad was a hot-headed. And we had parties. And we did school visits for people's houses and their homes. We used to have dances. And my mother would cook some stuff for the dancers. I remember making cakes. And we'd make the frosting and they'd put it with the snakes. It would take a long, long time to cook those eggs that way. And she would make sugar icing sometimes on cakes. And other things like that.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: How did you happen to start teaching school?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I went to normal school. And after that I taught school. I taught school, normal school one year and then I taught a year up in North Fork. And then I had to move to a one-room school. I had all the grades, but I'd never been in a school like that before in my life. I never heard of it. My training wasn't for a school like that, but I had to teach up there at Arlington Institute of Talent. And the next year I taught up there at Warner. I had a two-room, two-grade room. And I thought that was wonderful.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Did you continue teaching after you were married then? Yes.

speaker: Speaker 2
words: I taught... No. When I was married I was put out of teaching at Iowa School of the Entirety. I couldn't teach there.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: Oh, that was that period when if you were married you couldn't keep a job. How did you feel about that?

speaker: Speaker 2
words: Well, I didn't like it. But I didn't care. I went to a school that was good. It was a good school anyway. And then later I got to... That's a good one. And then I got a position at the... And then I dropped out. I taught at Kingston for about 22 years. And then the rest of the time I taught at the college.

speaker: Speaker 1
words: So, you were able to support yourself if anything would have happened to your husband.

speaker: Speaker 2
